#22821. How to Be Grateful for Your Morning Cup of Coffee

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1132 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Mindful ↗ Open Full Page

How to Be Grateful for Your Morning Cup of Coffee

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1132 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mindful

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We’re used to saying a quick “thank you,” to the barista who serves us coffee, or the kind stranger who holds the door open as we leave the cafe.
  • That’s a concept writer AJ Jacobs explores in his TED Talk and latest book, Thanks a Thousand, based on his journey to thank everyone involved in getting that daily cup of joe into his hands.
  • While Jacobs initially believed his choice to focus on a cup of coffee would be a simple task, he soon learned that there were hundreds of people involved in producing the hot drink most of us take for granted every day.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We’re used to saying a quick “thank you,” to the barista who serves us coffee, or the kind stranger who holds the door open as we leave the cafe. But how many people would you have to thank if you wanted to express gratitude to absolutely everyone responsible for your morning cup of coffee?

That’s a concept writer AJ Jacobs explores in his TED Talk and latest book, Thanks a Thousand, based on his journey to thank everyone involved in getting that daily cup of joe into his hands.

While Jacobs initially believed his choice to focus on a cup of coffee would be a simple task, he soon learned that there were hundreds of people involved in producing the hot drink most of us take for granted every day.

“I would thank the trucker who drove the coffee beans to the coffee shop, but he couldn’t have done his job without the road. So I would thank the people who paved the road, and then I would thank the people who made the asphalt for the pavement,” Jacobs says. “And I came to realize that my coffee, like so much else in the world, requires the combined work of a shocking number of people from all walks of life.”.

Why bother practicing gratitude in the first place? Jacobs, like many of us, found he often overlooked the positive aspects of his day and focused on the bad. By expressing gratitude when things went right, he was able to break out of his negative thoughts.

He explains: “It allowed me to focus on the hundreds of things that go right every day, as opposed to the three or four that go wrong.”.

Here are five lessons he learned when he set out to thank everyone responsible for his morning pick me up:.

Industry observers note that even if you start and end your gratitude journey by thanking your local barista (or local grocer, taxi driver, bartender, etc.) there’s a right way to do so. Namely: Look up from your phone and make eye contact.

“It reminds you, you’re dealing with a human being who has family and aspirations and embarrassing high school memories,” Jacobs indicates.

Taking a moment to connect with the person serving us can help us appreciate the people we interact with daily and show them that they are not “human vending machines.”.

“That little moment of connection is so crucial to both people’s humanity and happiness,” Jacobs says.

It has been revealed that as part of his mission to thank everyone, Jacobs reached out to Ed Kaufmann, who tests, tastes and selects coffee for a living. Jacobs was wowed by Kaufmann’s ability to notice all the small elements of flavor in coffee (notes of honeysuckle, for example) that most of us miss.

In our rush to finish our drink while getting ready for work, riding the subway, or taking notes in an office meeting, we often fail to slow down and truly notice what we’re tasting.

Industry observers note that “Inspired by Ed, I decided to really let the coffee sit on my tongue for five seconds,” Jacobs says. “We’re all busy, but I could spare five seconds, and really think about the texture and the acidity and the sweetness.”.

Doing so taught Jacobs the importance of savoring—the art of slowing down rather than consuming on autopilot.

Industry observers note that “This idea of savoring is so vital to gratitude,” he indicates. “Psychologists talk about how gratitude is about taking a moment and holding on to it as long as possible, and slowing down time so that life doesn’t go by in one massive blur, as it often does.”.

According to recent reports, when you consider all that goes into a cup of coffee—the beans, the sugar, the milk—it’s easy to overlook the cup itself. Yet Jacobs states one of the best conversations he had throughout his project was with a man who creates coffee cup lids.

“He says a bad lid can ruin your coffee,” Jacobs recounts. “That it can block the aroma, which is so notable to the experience. It made me realize there are hundreds of masterpieces all around us that we totally take for granted.”.

By taking the time to notice the little things we can “tap into that sense of wonder and enrich our lives,” Jacobs says.

Once he began his gratitude journey, Jacobs realized his project of writing thank you notes each day was creating a larger shift in his life: that when he saw the impact that “thank you” had on others, it began to affect him as well.

If you act as if you’re grateful, you eventually become grateful for real.

But that process often started with a lot of grumpiness and not a small amount of toil.

“I would wake up every morning in my default mood, which is grumpiness, but I would force myself to write a thank-you note, and then another, and then another,” he explains.

Despite not feeling grateful at first, Jacobs forced himself to go through the actions of gratitude and eventually noticed a transformation in his “default mood.”.

“What I found was that if you act as if you’re grateful, you eventually become grateful for real,” states Jacobs. “The power of our actions to change our mind is astounding. So often we think that thought changes behavior, but behavior very often changes our thought.”.

It has been revealed that for every one person Jacobs thanked, he learned there were many others he owed his gratitude to, people he would never be able to meet. It made him realize that sometimes, the best way to express gratitude for someone’s help is to help others in return.

In a recent development, “Some people worry that gratitude has a downside,” Jacobs says. “That we’ll be so grateful, that we’ll be complacent…Well, it turns out, the opposite is true. The research reveals that the more grateful you are, the more likely you are to help others.”.

For example, thanking the people whose job it is to provide clean water (essential to making coffee), caused him become involved with an organization called Dispensers for Safe Water whose mission is to provide drinking water to those in need.

“When you’re in a bad state, you’re often more focused on your own needs. But gratitude makes you want to pay it forward,” Jacobs concludes.

Nicole Bayes-Fleming holds an MSc in Gender, Media and Culture from the London School of Economics, where she researched the relationship between social media, knowledge production, and feminist social justice movements.

She has a bachelor’s in journalism, and has formerly worked as a digital editor and freelance reporter with bylines in Mindful Magazine, the Globe and Mail, FLARE, Ottawa Citizen, Ottawa Magazine, and HalifaxToday.ca.

Group biography follows Lee Miller, Pablo Picasso and friends on holiday in the South of France

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (796 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A group biography balances between a choir and a cacophony.
  • The individuals gathered in the Hotel Vaste Horizon in the French village of Mougins formed the chain of couples constituting this community: Eileen Agar and Joseph Bard, Nusch and Paul Éluard, Ady Fidelin and Man Ray, Dora Maar and Pablo Picasso, Lee Miller and Roland Penrose.
  • From this carefree and creative escape, Thomasson’s narrative plunges its participants into the war.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A group biography balances between a choir and a cacophony. Each person lies at the heart of a network, opening the potential for an exponential chain of many walk-on parts. Rooted in the photographs of what author Anna Thomasson rightly terms the “fleeting community” of a late summer holiday in 1937, A Vast Horizon succeeds remarkably in marshalling a complex tapestry of egos, events, ideals and disappointments.

The individuals gathered in the Hotel Vaste Horizon in the French village of Mougins formed the chain of couples constituting this community: Eileen Agar and Joseph Bard, Nusch and Paul Éluard, Ady Fidelin and Man Ray, Dora Maar and Pablo Picasso, Lee Miller and Roland Penrose. They were drawn to the South of France by their inter-linked friendships and by “le peintre soleil”, Agar’s witty characterisation of Picasso. As Picasso urged everyone to work, half the witnesses took photographs. Maar, Man Ray and Miller were the relaxing professionals; snapshots were added by Agar and Penrose. Thomasson has searched through this rich, if scattered visual archive of a moment through which photography (as Roland Barthes recognised in Camera Lucida) “mechanically repeats what could never be repeated existentially”. Their hedonism caught in this moment defied the political instability and totalitarianism, with civil war already a year old in Spain.

From this carefree and creative escape, Thomasson’s narrative plunges its participants into the war. For each of them it constituted a restructuring of values—not as hoped for by the Surrealists, but as enforced by the destructive triumphalism of Nazi extremism. Here the account turns to Paul Éluard’s transformation of a love poem for Nusch into a litany for “liberty” that captured the spirit of resistance (copies were even dropped over Occupied France by the RAF). Equally powerful was Miller’s reportage of the savagery of combat and, eventually, the revelations of the concentration camps. In this way, the book touches upon the transience of bodies captured in photography: those at Hotel Vaste Horizon were willingly posed for the camera and exchanged in partnerships, before growing fragile through wartime deprivation.

Sources indicate that there was no reciprocal gathering in the post-war period. As a result, Thomasson traces the endgames, as each of the participants ages in varying degrees of dignity, creativity and despair. Those bodies displayed on the beach in southern France become the distant, optimistic opposite to the tragic, haunting corpses of Buchenwald; it is little wonder that Miller, the photographer in both cases, would never fully recover from the experience of witnessing such deliberate inhumanity.

Picnic of stars: Lee Miller’s 1937 photo of (left to right) Nusch and Paul Éluard, Roland Penrose, Man Ray and Ady Fidelin.

It has been revealed that while the lives of many of these central figures are, to varying degrees, familiar—from autobiographies (Agar, Man Ray, Penrose) and biographies (Éluard, Miller, Picasso)—Thomasson’s synthesis draws on recent research and extensive reading. A particular strength is the rebalancing of longstanding gender biases and assumptions. The repositioning of Ady Fidelin, the double-marginalised Guadeloupean woman, is especially timely; drawing on fresh scholarship, she is given greater presence and somewhat rescued from simply being Man Ray’s model. Nusch Éluard is also brought more sharply into focus. Substantial traces of these women’s own voices remain to be found, however, confining them to an unknowability ascribed to their devotion to their partners, although this may be overstated in the suggestion that, in 1946, Nusch Éluard “died in the service of Paul [Éluard]’s pursuit of freedom”.

In a recent development, late on Thomasson cites Emily Dickinson’s belief that veracity is “more affecting, if told indirectly”. This emerges as a foundational conceit in a volume inspired by photographs but in which only four are reproduced. Instead of showing, the author presents often highly evocative descriptions of what she sees in a wide range of images that the reader is not shown. This is a surprising decision for a narrative stimulated, as we are told, by the author being drawn into “their distant world by their photographs”.

It has been revealed that with such a limitation on images, the book’s cover photograph assumes disproportionate significance. Where the British edition favours Agar’s photograph of Maar, Picasso and the Éluards at Juan-les-Pins, Miller’s picnic photograph of “half-naked women sitting among fully clothed men”—the jarring nature of which introduces the whole narrative—appears on the cover of the US edition. Although unaltered when reproduced inside the volume, on the cover the half-naked torsos are rather ineptly airbrushed. That the publishers chose to manipulate a famous 90-year-old image seems an unfortunate undermining of an otherwise compelling narrative of artists embracing freedom before disaster struck.

ª A Vast Horizon: Artists and Lovers, Freedom and War, by Anna Thomasson, published by Pegasus Books, 304pp, 4 b/w reproductions, $29.95 (hb), 7 July.

A collection of protected landscapes, united through their biodiversity and fragility. Lantern was appointed to bring these organisations together and better define and promote their common goals to preserve, restore and enhance the local life, landscapes and wildlife of the Norfolk Coast.

We helped to define this unique destination’s strategic positioning, whilst delivering a latest visual and verbal identity to promote the responsible exploration of the region, ensuring it’s here for everyone, forever.

Hiking, cycling and kayaking through protected landscapes.

Recent findings suggest that to fully understand what makes Norfolk so special and distinct, we embarked on a four-day immersion trip as a team. We hiked, cycled, bird watched, and conducted several interviews with local families and visitors.

It was crucial for us to discover the genuine essence of Norfolk and what it means for the local community and stakeholders who call it home, as well as identifying the key areas that require greater protection.

It has been revealed that norfolk’s coastal landscapes, seascapes and communities have rhythms like a heartbeat. They move across millennia, change with the seasons, and even differ day to day. Waterways widen and wander. Wildlife migrates and hibernates. Farmland flourishes and lies fallow. This is a living coast in perpetual motion. This is a living coast in perpetual motion. Often wild yet sometimes serene.

Our newly introduced strategy celebrates this wild, natural backdrop and all that defines it; land and sea, nature and community, they all live together in gentle harmony. And like every living thing, this delicate place deserves to be respected and protected.

Inspired by the sweeping landscapes of Norfolk’s coast and creeks we brought together the N and C of the brand name creating a unique symbol, paired with a visual language that’s full of energy and alive with nature.

Industry observers note that reflected through the interplay of type, image and illustration, we put the audience deep into the experience. To further reflect the landscape we directed an off-season photoshoot, encouraging sustainable exploration throughout the year.

Letting the Film Breathe: A Conversation with Filmmaker Julie Bayer Salzman

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2889 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mindful

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, in 2013, Julie Bayer Salzman’s five-year-old son came home from kindergarten talking about his prefrontal cortex and his amygdala.
  • According to recent reports, just Breathe grew into Mindful Shorts, an ongoing series of experiential documentaries that follow mindfulness across the life span.
  • Former Mindful editor Ava Whitney-Coulter first spoke with Salzman in 2024.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, in 2013, Julie Bayer Salzman’s five-year-old son came home from kindergarten talking about his prefrontal cortex and his amygdala. She was so struck that she signed up for the same mindfulness course his school used to train its teachers. During one of her meditations, she pictured a short film. That film became Just Breathe, in which elementary school kids describe how mindfulness helps them work with anger. It was featured on Oprah’s Super Soul Sunday and has since been translated into six languages and shown in classrooms around the world.

According to recent reports, just Breathe grew into Mindful Shorts, an ongoing series of experiential documentaries that follow mindfulness across the life span. The five films so far cover anger in childhood, anxiety in middle school, depression in high school, addiction in midlife, and grief in the elder years. Made with her husband and creative partner, cinematographer Josh Salzman, through their firm Wavecrest Films, the series is funded by donations and offered free to anyone who needs it.

Former Mindful editor Ava Whitney-Coulter first spoke with Salzman in 2024. After the recent release of Bayer’s latest film, Broken & Beautiful, Mindful Chief Editor Siri Myhrom caught up with her at her home in LA. They spoke about what it’s like to work on creative projects with her partner, what advertising taught her, how her practice shows up on set, and what she’s learned from the people at the heart of her newest films.

It has been revealed that siri Myhrom: You spent more than a decade producing commercial campaigns before directing your own work. What did advertising teach you about storytelling, and what did you have to unlearn?

It has been revealed that julie Bayer Salzman: Advertising taught me the importance of strong visuals in nonfiction filmmaking. Sometimes documentary filmmakers don’t place as much value on the visual style as they do on simply capturing the action unfolding in order to tell the best story, and of course that makes a lot of sense in some respect, because story is everything; however, film is a visual medium, and a documentary needs to be more than journalistic. It’s worth taking time to capture reality as beautifully as you can. That noted, sometimes when documentaries look too slick, it can be a distraction. To me it’s notable to find the balance.

We ask ourselves a simple question: What kind of value does it add to our shared human experience on this planet?

Commercials also taught me how to distill a story to its essence in a short amount of time. And yet, taken too far, that can be a detriment to any story. I had to unlearn to some extent the tendency to truncate a scene out of learned impatience, or playing into the audience’s short attention span. I don’t know if you’ve noticed, but there is not a lot of breathing space in a commercial!

This may seem corny or cliché, but when I started practicing mindfulness, I actually started to lean more into the idea of allowing a film to breathe. As I was learning to breathe more consciously myself, my filmmaking style started to evolve differently, more experientially—slowing the pace, and allowing more pauses between the thoughts or statements.

According to recent reports, SM: Wavecrest’s mission is to make content with a positive social impact, and you’ve said you choose projects carefully so you don’t add to the noise. How do you decide whether a project is worth making?

Recent findings suggest that JBS: We ask ourselves a simple question: What kind of value does it add to our shared human experience on this planet? Meaning: Does the project help us evolve collectively? Change the way we see the world? Inspire us to be better humans? Cultivate connection with nature or other humans? Laugh? If none of those things, then we’ll pass, thanks.

It has been revealed that SM: You and Josh are married as well as creative partners. How do you divide the work, and how do you handle creative disagreements?

JBS: We’re incredibly lucky to have very complementary skill sets, while often sharing feelings as well as values. I’m substantial-picture; he’s details. I’ve got a million ideas and my antennae up at all times, taking in everything around me. I “see” the film conceptually, and have my producer skill set from years in commercials, therefore I tend to take the lead as director and producer; but he’s the cinematographer, and I trust him implicitly to capture my vision in the best possible way.

In a recent development, I can’t say we have creative disagreements, because honestly, we don’t. We respect each other’s strengths in a really beautiful way. It’s a unique creative synergy that I do not take for granted.

When it’s time to edit, I lay out the story, then pass it to him to sculpt the fine details that I usually have no patience for, like on which exact frame to place a cut. He enjoys tedium in a way I don’t.

I can’t say we have creative disagreements, because honestly, we don’t. We respect each other’s strengths in a really beautiful way. It’s a unique creative synergy that I do not take for granted.

SM: When did mindfulness become part of your personal life, and when did you realize it could be the subject of your films?

JBS: Mindfulness became part of my life when my son started kindergarten in 2013. He came home at the age of five, talking about his prefrontal cortex and his amygdala, thanks to the social-emotional learning curriculum at his school, and I immediately enrolled in the course that the school’s principal used to train the teachers. While meditating one day, I envisioned the first film in the Mindful Shorts series, Just Breathe, and promptly made that film. Once I saw the success it was having, I realized that people were hungry for this type of learning, and the rest of the series evolved from there.

It has been revealed that SM: You describe the Mindful Shorts as “experiential” films. What does that mean to you, and how do you design a film that viewers experience rather than just watch?

Industry observers note that JBS: It means artfully crafting a film that results more in an embodied experience for the audience, rather than a passive viewing. We don’t conform to traditional standards in order to tell a story; we shape it in such a way that we hope the viewers walk away from the film feeling different energetically than they did at the start. That there is an actual impact on the nervous system—a sense of calm, of understanding—a certain kind of peace within.

Industry observers note that when I’m interviewing people, I rarely consult my list of predetermined interview questions. Instead, I like to have a more intimate conversation, where the responses lead to more questions, rather than just asking questions in search of answers.

SM: Does your own mindfulness practice change how you behave on set, such as how you listen, when you stay quiet, or how you handle the unexpected?

JBS: Absolutely. The quality of presence, of attention, are much greater now. I’m far less in my head than I used to be, and it allows for more spontaneity and creative problem solving. I think my practice allows me to be much more fluid and present than I used to be.

Sources indicate that when I’m interviewing people, I rarely consult my list of predetermined interview questions. Instead, I like to have a more intimate conversation, where the responses lead to more questions, rather than just asking questions in search of answers. The goal is not to cross items off a list; it’s to have an experience with the process itself.

SM: Mindfulness is an inner experience, and film is a visual medium. How do you show something that happens inside a person?

JBS: When you’re talking about something in one’s interior world, the exterior world must match it. Yes, film itself is a visual medium, but filmmaking as an art form is multisensory. In addition to having a distinct visual style, we place an enormous value on sound—ambient noise, music, everything—as well as on editorial pacing. It all must reflect the emotional tone behind what is being said, the changes and transformation that a character is going through when they are learning how to mindfully show up in the world.

We are not intimidating folks; I think we are warm and open by nature.

In a recent development, SM: Your films are unscripted and often feature people talking about very personal struggles. How do you create the kind of safety and trust that lets people be that open on camera?

Recent findings suggest that JBS: I’m not sure I can answer this question, because it’s not something I consciously do. I think it’s mostly inherent to who both Josh and I are as human beings. We are not intimidating folks; I think we are warm and open by nature. I like to think that people just instinctively trust that we are safe to be vulnerable with, that we emanate an air of security.

In a recent development, SM: The series follows mindfulness from childhood through old age, moving from anger, to anxiety, depression, addiction, and grief. Was that structure planned from the beginning, or did it develop as you went?

It has been revealed that JBS: Both. After the success of Just Breathe (on anger and elementary school kids), I recognized there was more work to be done. I awoke at 3 a.m., seeing the rest of the series in my head, so I grabbed my journal, sat on the couch, and wrote the progression of the films in a way that made sense to me.

It has been revealed that what’s after elementary school? Middle school, when we start to name “stress.” I immediately thought about how people tend to project their anxieties on the world around them, and decided we had to project images on our subjects for that film (which eventually became Release). And then I started to think about high school, when we start to name “Depression,” and I began conjuring up what that film (Into Light) might look like. Next I started to think about the stage of middle life, when addiction tends to surface and become a problem for many. And on and on…it was a middle-of-the-night revelation of sorts.

The two most recent Mindful Shorts carry the series into adulthood. A Good Day (32 minutes) explores mindfulness and addiction in midlife, and won at the Real HeArt Film Festival. Broken & Beautiful (23 minutes) centers on Sandy Phillips, who turned to mindfulness after the death of her daughter, and took top honors at LA Shorts.

SM: A Good Day takes on addiction in midlife and is the longest Mindful Short so far. Why did this subject need more time than the earlier films?

In a recent development, JBS: Addiction is often the result of the unprocessed experiences that the earlier films delve into (anger, anxiety, depression, and trauma), and it’s something we don’t often deal with until we’re middle aged, so as I was editing the film, I felt the need to go deeper into it, covering ground I thought was necessary in order to be more comprehensive, which naturally resulted in a longer film. I guess it’s fair to say that the topic itself seemed to dictate the length of the film.

When you’re young, a loss (like a breakup with a first love, for example) seems like the end of the world, but older people know it’s just one of many, and that life is full of losses.

SM: Broken & Beautiful is about a particular kind of grief, the terrible loss of a child, and, more generally, grief in the elder years. What did you learn from older subjects about presence and loss that younger subjects couldn’t have taught you?

Recent findings suggest that JBS: When you’re young, a loss (like a breakup with a first love, for example) seems like the end of the world, but older people know it’s just one of many, and that life is full of losses. The subject of Broken & Beautiful, Sandy Phillips, possesses a certain wisdom that only comes with age. That’s not to say that someone younger couldn’t speak to loss or grief, but she has lived through so much—and she started practicing mindfulness specifically to help herself process and navigate the death of her daughter.

It has been revealed that that kind of perspective is rarely inherent in any one person’s being; it takes real time and intention to cultivate and embody it. Her particular quality of presence and attention is something that is earned, and learned, over years.

SM: Did making Broken & Beautiful affect how you deal with grief in your own life?

It has been revealed that JBS: I think it impacted Josh more than me so far, as he had to deal with the unexpected death of his mother from a heart attack in 2012—a trauma that took him a long time to process. I think I can speak for him, though, when I say he no longer sees death as an ending to a person or the relationship with that person—something that was very difficult for him to accept earlier.

And then, sadly and tragically, the young kintsugi artist in Broken & Beautiful, Fumika Tanokashira, died suddenly last spring (2026), and I’m not sure I can quite put my finger on it but there was something profound about it all—the fact that she is the one showing us metaphorically, via kintsugi, how to put our lives back together after a terrible loss, and here she is the one now gone. It just leaves me speechless every time I think about it.

For some people, anecdotes are insufficient, and I understand why.

It has been revealed that SM: Your next film is about trauma in young adults and will focus on the science behind mindfulness. Why add a scientific angle now, and how do you plan to balance research with personal stories?

It has been revealed that JBS: I haven’t been awoken by a vision for that one yet! But I trust it will come…it always does. Sometimes it’s imagined ahead of time; sometimes it just emerges organically during the process of making a film. We shall see what the future holds.

Industry observers note that but to answer the question of “why add a scientific angle now”: because skeptics still exist. For some people, anecdotes are insufficient, and I understand why. Proof must be in the data. Well, there’s plenty of data out there, and I intend to do something with it. I just have to find the right people who wish to collaborate on making that film. I know they’re out there.

SM: The Mindful Shorts are funded through donations and offered for free. What does that model make possible, and what does it make harder?

It has been revealed that JBS: What the model makes possible is grant money, because the series is produced as not-for-profit. We also retain full ownership and creative control of the content. There’s a certain satisfaction in knowing that anyone who needs the films can access them for free, even if it takes years to find them!

It has been revealed that yet the downside of that all is that we don’t have access to “investor” money. Investors want to know they’ll get their money back and more (spoiler alert: they won’t). It’s also harder to get third-party distribution when you go the not-for-profit model, so we self-distribute on YouTube, Vimeo, and other social media platforms (as well as of course have the films up on our website, Wavecrest Films). It’s certainly not the most lucrative way of doing things, but it feels right given the nature of what we’re trying to do.

Recent findings suggest that everything stems from awareness. Without real personal growth on a larger societal level, the Earth will continue to suffer.

SM: You’ve urged your audience to work on being better humans because the planet demands it. How do your environmental work and your mindfulness work connect for you?

JBS: Our first film, Time & Tide (2006), was on climate change in the South Pacific, and for years afterward, the environment was top on our list of topics we felt we, as filmmakers, must address. But then I started to think that there was no point trying to convince people to change their actions without teaching them first about self-awareness.

Everything stems from awareness. Without real personal growth on a larger societal level, the Earth will continue to suffer. We have to heal ourselves first if we wish to heal the planet. I do firmly believe though that once there’s a larger sea change of consciousness, planetary health will improve—one person at a time.

Siri Liv Myhrom is a writer, editor, and certified spiritual director from Minneapolis, MN, where she has lived with her husband and two young daughters for 20 years. Her meditation practices include cycling, cold dipping in the nearby lake, and playing the ukulele (low skill but lots of gusto). She is the Editor at Mindful.

Your Intuition Is Smarter Than You Think

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sometimes these signals feel obvious, like a burst of excitement in your chest or butterflies in your stomach.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You may recognize that quiet, inner pull that comes when you least expect it, perhaps as a sense of unease that makes you change plans at the last minute, only to find out later that you narrowly missed something dangerous. Or you may feel drawn toward certain people or places without quite knowing why, only to discover later that those connections opened doors to fresh opportunities.

Sometimes these signals feel obvious, like a burst of excitement in your chest or butterflies in your stomach. Other times, they show up as a quiet sense of simply knowing what to do. Whether they’re instantaneous or linger over time, they may be signs of your intuition in action.

If you don’t feel very in tune with your intuition, there’s good news: Each day, you have the opportunity to turn inward, notice your thoughts, emotions, and bodily sensations, and listen to what your inner voice might be telling you. Over time, this practice of self-awareness can become a habit that helps you live more authentically and fully.

Intuition stems from our nervous system, emotions, and unconscious processes working together to help us make sense of the world.

Intuition stems from our nervous system, emotions, and unconscious processes working together to help us make sense of the world. Our body’s sensory networks are always at work gathering information from our environment, finding patterns from past experiences, and directing our present-day thinking and decisions.

Through our senses, our nervous system gathers information and sends signals to the brain. Regions like the amygdala help us rapidly detect potential threats, while the prefrontal cortex, which handles complex reasoning and decision-making, helps us interpret information more deliberately.

Research suggests that our brains can begin detecting and interpreting subtle facial expressions in a fraction of a second.

In a recent development, that first, quick assessment happens remarkably fast. For instance, research suggests that our brains can begin detecting and interpreting subtle facial expressions in a fraction of a second.

Sources indicate that intuition differs from instinct, which involves automatic responses that can help protect us from danger, including reactions like fight, flight, or freeze. While instinctive responses are largely automatic, intuition draws on our past life experiences and learned patterns to help us make sense of what we encounter in daily life. Although both can feel immediate, intuitive judgments are not always accurate and may also reflect learned biases or assumptions.

Sources indicate that intuition can feel like a gut feeling that is hard to put into words. This is because our brain is able to look for patterns between old memories and present-day situations, using useful takeaways from the past to guide us now. This process can also include implicit, unconscious memories that we may have thought we’d forgotten.

If the brain is key to processing intuition, then why do we often associate it with a “gut feeling?”.

If the brain is key to processing intuition, then why do we often associate it with a “gut feeling?” Part of the explanation lies in the gut-brain axis, the complex communication network connecting our brain and digestive system. The walls of our digestive tract contain a network of millions of neurons that make up the enteric nervous system, or ENS.

The ENS is often called our “second brain” because it can regulate many digestive functions independently of the central nervous system. Through the gut-brain axis, digestive processes can also interact with systems involved in mood and emotion. Research has linked gastrointestinal inflammation and changes in gut function with symptoms of depression and anxiety. Most of the body’s serotonin is also produced in the digestive tract, although it doesn’t directly enter the brain. Researchers are still exploring the complex relationship between gut health and mental well-being.

This gut-brain connection helps explain why we might experience a sinking feeling in the pit of our stomach when something doesn’t feel quite right.

All day long, our minds are hard at work integrating rational thought with emotional intelligence (EQ). EQ helps us to become aware of and understand both our emotions and those of others. It’s a type of intelligence we can develop through emotion regulation practice, expanding our emotional vocabulary, and approaching feelings as clues to something instead of an end product.

To be in our wise mind allows us to stay aware of feelings like fear and anger without judging them, or acting on them impulsively.

EQ can help us manage stress, notice our assumptions, and respond more thoughtfully to difficult emotions, such as those that arise after a tense conversation. It helps us pause and remain mindful during challenging moments, and also as we choose our next steps. Developing emotional intelligence may also support our ability to recover from stressful experiences.

According to recent reports, in Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT), combining emotional awareness with rational thinking is known as accessing our wise mind. To be in our wise mind allows us to stay aware of feelings like fear and anger without judging them, or acting on them impulsively. Instead of automatically acting on our first reaction, we can ground ourselves while tackling emotionally painful situations.

Wisdom and living authentically are closely connected.

Wisdom and living authentically are closely connected. As the ancient Greek maxim “Know thyself” suggests, self-knowledge is an crucial part of wisdom. By understanding our deeper motivations, core needs, and cherished values, we can make more intentional decisions that reflect who we are and what matters most to us.

Sources indicate that family systems therapist Virginia Satir connected personal authenticity to congruence between our internal reality and outward actions. This alignment can support our emotional well-being and help us act in ways that reflect our values. Incongruence, however, may leave us with a nagging sense that things are not quite right. Noticing incongruence in real time can help us to adjust and choose to do what feels more authentic to us and who we wish to be.

Sometimes, traumatic experiences can make it harder to recognize or trust our intuition, particularly when painful memories leave us feeling fearful or unsafe. Common trauma responses, such as hypervigilance to danger, will tax our nervous system, making it difficult to access the balanced perspective of our wise mind.

Trauma-based responses, such as anticipating negative outcomes in uncertain situations, can contribute to doubting our intuition and avoiding risks.

Trauma-based responses, such as anticipating negative outcomes in uncertain situations, can contribute to doubting our intuition and avoiding risks. Similarly, depression can affect our self-esteem and confidence, informing how we interpret fresh situations as more negative. Holding hope for a better future might require noticing the positive patterns that run through our lives, and accessing support to process what we have gone through.

Recent findings suggest that social pressure can also make us second-guess ourselves. For example, growing up with family expectations to defer to others and put their needs first might make us believe that prioritizing our own needs is selfish. Similarly, other people’s ideas of what success looks like can make us overlook our own aspirations, such as the desire to pursue a different career path.

Industry observers note that we may become more aware of these pressures as we get older. Hospice nurse Bronnie Ware identified five common regrets her patients shared toward the end of their lives:.

These reflections offer a reminder of the importance of making choices that align with what matters most to us.

Getting to know ourselves—our preferences, desires, and even dreams—requires making time to turn inward. A helpful practice for building the habit of self-reflecting is time in peaceful solitude. Time alone may encourage mind-wandering and daydreaming, activities associated with the brain’s default mode network, which plays a role in reflection, imagination, and our sense of self.

Quiet may even have benefits for brain health. In one study, mice exposed to periods of silence developed more immature neurons in the hippocampus, a region involved in memory and learning. Though similar effects haven’t been established in humans, the presence of young neurons in the mice is a sign of brain plasticity. And while quiet moments may sometimes feel boring, they can also create space for reflection, creativity and upcoming ideas.

Other practices, such as spending time in nature, journaling, meditation, engaging in spiritual reflection, and limiting technology, may also strengthen our intuition and self-awareness, as we remember who we are and what we care about the most.

Clarity about our personal values is another entryway to deepening intuition. In Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT), values help guide meaningful action and provide direction as we navigate life’s uncertainties. They can guide our daily actions much like an inner compass would—keeping us focused on long-term goals.

Industry observers note that knowing our values helps us remember how we want to show up during challenging times and stay grounded when stress feels overwhelming. Values can take many forms, from nurturing relationships, to cultivating personal qualities, or finding greater joy and fulfillment in everyday life. Naming your values and writing them down may help you distinguish between choices rooted in what matters to you and those driven primarily by fear, particularly when clarity feels hard to find.

Recent findings suggest that psychotherapy can provide an intentional, supportive space where you can go inward. Therapy can also help us explore how past experiences shape our reactions, making it easier to distinguish familiar emotional patterns from what we’re noticing in the present. There are many evidence-based therapies that can help support trauma recovery, managing symptoms of anxiety and depression, and building a stronger sense of self:.

Each time we pause, turn inward, and honor what we notice inside, we can build a more honest and trusting relationship with ourselves.

Industry observers note that thinking back to the gut feelings we began with—the caution that turned out to be right, and the inner pull that led toward new possibilities—we can see how these experiences may reflect more than coincidence. Instead, they’re signs that our nervous system, emotional intellect, mental pattern-finding, and lived experience are all working together to shape our perceptions and decisions.

It has been revealed that learning to trust our intuition’s guidance can take practice, particularly if difficult experiences have caused us to doubt it. But each time we pause, turn inward, and honor what we notice inside, we can build a more honest and trusting relationship with ourselves. Over time, what once felt like a faint signal may become a steady, recognizable voice that helps us move forward with greater confidence. Our capacity for intuitive wisdom is always there, and the invitation is simply to listen.

Marian Ting, LMFT, is a therapist and writer specializing in mood disorders, complex trauma, and AAPI mental health. She is pursuing a PhD in depth psychology at Pacifica Graduate Institute, with research interests in the synergies between self-compassion and authentic selfhood. Her writing has been published by Psychotherapy Networker, the Anxiety and Depression Association of America, and Psychedelic Support, among others. She believes beauty and struggle can coexist, and that honest self-reflection is a form of healing.

AI helps conservators uncover lost details in William Merritt Chase painting

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, the newly restored painting, which is part of the collection of the Parrish Art Museum in Water Mill, New York, will be on display in its exhibition William Merritt Chase and Walter Granville-Smith: American Impressionists of the East End (14 November-21 March 2027).
  • A Comfortable Corner depicts a woman reclining in an elaborately furnished interior, dressed in a deep blue kimono and holding an uchiwa fan.“A Comfortable Corner is an important work within William Merritt Chase’s oeuvre as it depicts a specific moment in 19th-century art and Chase’s own period with influences of art and design from Japan,” states Kaitlin Halloran, the museum’s associate curator.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that when William Merritt Chase’s painting A Comfortable Corner (around 1888) entered the conservation studio, the painting was carrying more than a century of history on its surface—including the interventions of conservators who had treated it decades earlier. Artificial intelligence (AI) contributed to a restoration endeavour that has peeled back some of those interventions.

In a recent development, the newly restored painting, which is part of the collection of the Parrish Art Museum in Water Mill, New York, will be on display in its exhibition William Merritt Chase and Walter Granville-Smith: American Impressionists of the East End (14 November-21 March 2027). The Parrish has an especially deep connection to Chase, who was not only a prominent figure in Gilded Age New York but also spent time on Long Island’s East End, where the museum is located. Today, the Parrish holds a substantial body of Chase’s work, alongside archival material donated by the artist’s family.

A Comfortable Corner depicts a woman reclining in an elaborately furnished interior, dressed in a deep blue kimono and holding an uchiwa fan.“A Comfortable Corner is an important work within William Merritt Chase’s oeuvre as it depicts a specific moment in 19th-century art and Chase’s own period with influences of art and design from Japan,” states Kaitlin Halloran, the museum’s associate curator.

Over the years, at least two restorations substantially altered the appearance of the painting, including a significant effort in the 1960s. Among the changes made were the addition of a heavyweight, almost burlap-like lining, retouching and blotchy inpainting, and the use of uneven varnishes. Some of these interventions changed the surface texture of various areas or discoloured over time. Working with conservator Suzanne Siano and her team at Modern Art Conservation, the museum set out to determine what restoration was needed to get the painting ready for the exhibition.

It has been revealed that A crucial piece of evidence to guide this process arrived in the form of an early photograph of the painting. The black-and-white image, understood to have been taken before the 1960s restoration, showed that more of the composition had once been visible than what had survived in the painting. The work had apparently been reduced in size during the 1960s restoration, perhaps to fit a new stretcher or because damaged edges were folded over and effectively removed.

Conservators from Modern Art Conservation with William Merritt Chase's A Comfortable Corner (The Blue Kimono) (around 1888) Photo: Lindsey Del Rio for Modern Art Conservation.

Sources indicate that the photograph also revealed details in the composition that had disappeared. A curl of hair beneath the sitter’s ear was missing; parts of a decorative screen had become faint or vanished; and some delicate passages had been overpainted with heavier marks. The conservation team also found evidence of pentimenti—changes made by Chase himself—that were not apparent in the earlier photograph, adding another layer of complexity.

“It is difficult to establish whether all of these changes resulted from earlier conservation,” Siano tells The Art Newspaper. “Some of it may have stemmed from a misreading of what the conservator was seeing. They may have been cleaning toward what they believed to be the original surface when, in fact, some of what they removed may have been changes or additions made by the artist.”.

Using AI, the historical photograph was combined with a colour image of the painting to create a composite showing areas where the two diverged.

“Although we are reasonably adept with Photoshop, we felt it was worth seeing what AI could offer,” Siano notes. “It proved very helpful, largely because of its speed. It was not instantaneous, but it was considerably faster than assembling the comparison manually.”.

In a recent development, the resulting image helped the team identify areas that warranted closer examination. One vital discovery concerned Chase’s signature, which had become extremely faint, with some of its letters apparently covered by overpaint. Because Chase’s signature is relatively abstract, Siano believes it may have been mistaken for part of the carpet pattern during the earlier restoration.

The project, supported by a Bank of America grant, illustrates both the possibilities and the limitations of AI in conservation. “Tasks that once took considerable time can be completed more quickly, and AI can provide additional information for us to weigh,” Siano says. “Ultimately, however, conservation is carried out by a highly skilled individual or team, and we do not expect that to change.”.

Siano stresses that they did not simply reinstate every discrepancy identified by the software. The historical photograph was neither high-resolution nor necessarily a record of the painting’s earliest state. Instead, the information the photograph provided was assessed alongside magnified examination, ultraviolet imaging, knowledge of Chase’s materials, and comparison with his other works.

It has been revealed that “Conservation is a combination of science, art history, craft, manual skill and artistry,” Siano notes. “AI is none of those things.”.

It has been revealed that the Chase painting was the first time Siano’s studio had used AI as an aid in the conservation of a painting. “In terms of determining how to conserve a painting, we think AI’s use will remain very case-specific. We do expect it to become increasingly valuable as a research tool, however: for example, in helping to locate historical images or relevant source material.”.

Ultimately, Siano says, “the judgments conservators make are nuanced and subtle, and we doubt those qualities can be replicated by a machine”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Very often, the thought of practicing a kind, friendly presence that allows us to connect with pain rather than turn away from it seems counter-intuitive, doesn’t it? Generally, when we come into contact with something painful or scary, our habitual tendency is to push it away, and to try to get away from it out of self-preservation. This is not your fault. This is biology.

We are the ancestors of the nervous animals, so achieving a kind of intimacy with our difficulties doesn’t exactly come naturally. It’s hard for us to imagine that the things we’ve been battling with our whole lives could be sources of awakening. And it’s so easy to judge our experiences, essentially holding it against ourselves that we are the way we are.

Industry observers note that add to that, the many ways to opt out of actually caring for ourselves in our contemporary culture. Maybe we worry we’re being self-indulgent or even come to see ourselves as inconveniences. It’s so easy to slip into judgment.

With compassion practice we open up to this tender space. And when that opening happens, we find there’s actually room for the life that’s right here, right now. So, I ask you to go easy on yourself as we venture into this territory of giving ourselves compassion.

What is the real cost of being at war with ourselves, or some part of ourselves?

According to recent reports, we come by it all so honestly. But let’s explore: What is the real cost of being at war with ourselves, or some part of ourselves? And what does it really feel like when we wage that war? How much are our experiences bringing to us, and how much are we bringing to our experiences?

According to recent reports, consider this: Our response to whatever arises is where we put our attention—that’s what we actually have influence over. We can’t control what arises. We do have some power over where we place our attention.

Many practitioners talk about this in terms of the “second arrow.” That’s when we take something that’s already difficult and multiply that by our resistance to it. And this can be far more painful than the initial feeling itself.

This is the formula: Experience x Resistance = Suffering.

According to recent reports, so, how do we hold ourselves with some compassion? “Suffering” is a really big word. In light of all that’s going on in the world, it’s easy to feel like we can dismiss what we’re dealing with personally. But I think we have to include ourselves and whatever difficulties we’re dealing with. The mind is always saying, “Well, at least, you know, at least…”—and you fill in the blank. At least it’s not this, at least it’s not that. I don’t know about you, but I can feel kind of bullied into gratitude when I’m not willing to meet what’s difficult with some compassion. Let’s accept, then, that resistance is normal. Resistance gets to be here, too.

Pain can be in our lives in countless ways—and all of it is difficult. Each one of us has been touched by grief, loss, countless struggles. Those things in and of themselves are difficult for many of us to navigate. But even harder than those things is when we regard what has happened, or is happening, as our fault.

We don’t have to defend our pain or judge ourselves. I see it with my two-year-old son. Sometimes he’s just screaming. Something is just really, really bothering him. It doesn’t matter what it is. I know what he needs. He needs a hug. He needs to be held. He needs care. He needs loving attention.

That’s what we’re going to do in this practice: hold ourselves with that same kind of care. We’re going to allow ourselves to kiss our own wounds the way we would for anyone we care about.

According to recent reports, we start with a willingness to have contact with the pain and soften to it, not resist it. We do that by tuning into our body and the sensations that are present. Is there a temperature shift? A throbbing? Is it moving? Is there a centre; are their edges? Are there places that it’s not?

Industry observers note that if it becomes overwhelming, we can allow our awareness to go to the part of our experience that’s not activated. We can visit where this pain lives in our bodies, and we can come back to a place of calm if it gets to be too much.

Recent findings suggest that bringing our curiosity to this is key. Not “why is this happening to me?” or the story we might be building around it, but what is the felt sense of this pain? This is the power of mindfulness—the ability to cultivate a clearer view of what’s coming up and therefore not be blindsided by it or lost in it.

We’re looking for two components in this practice, then: willingness and seeing clearly. Simply put, when we bring compassion home to include ourselves, our job is to honor the hurt. This isn’t easy. In fact, it’s very rare for us to meet ourselves in that place. But if we don’t, we’re losing out on living a considerable portion of our lives.

As we talked about last week, the strategy here is to widen our circle of care as we go. We started with those dearest to us; now we’re going focus on ourselves. Next week we will hold neutral people in mind and then we’ll hold everyone, including difficult people. I love the sequence, but sometimes I feel like when I’m practicing, I can be all four of those categories of people. Sometimes I’m an easy person to care about. Sometimes it’s difficult to hold myself with compassion. Sometimes I feel pretty neutral.

I encourage you to reflect on when you feel you need love the most. For me, it’s particularly when I mess up. And when we don’t feel like we can meet ourselves, isn’t that when we really see what kind of lovers we are? Is it conditional—is it as long as I act right? What we want to do here is widen the berth of where we’re willing to meet ourselves.

Sources indicate that I want to re-emphasize here: It’s vital not to use any part of the practice to judge ourselves. What we’re trying to do is give ourselves a pardon. This is how we can meet ourselves where we feel most unmet.

I find it helpful to note what’s arising as I’m doing this compassion practice. It helps me to see better what my relationship is to that pain. This also helps me to see this as something that’s passing through my awareness. It’s not who I am. I find that distinction very helpful.

To put it another way, we’re trying not to take any of this personally. We realize we can practice with just about anything if we’re not taking it personally. Whether it’s stress, frustration, pain: nothing has to be outside our care. Maybe we feel like we’ve been through too much pain, or not enough—it doesn’t really matter why we’re in pain, just that we can acknowledge that there is stuff that is painful.

Industry observers note that remember, too, that we’re inviting spaciousness around this pain we’re finding. The pain is not the only thing happening here. This is the alchemy of presence. It helps us approach the very difficulties that we’ve been desperately trying to avoid so that they can become the sources of our awakening, of our wisdom, of equanimity.

OK, let’s stop reading the menu and eat some of the food.

Sources indicate that located in the heart of the Mexican city of Hermosillo, Sonora, you will find Champ, a small boutique hotel. The street on which it is located is Campodónico, the surname of recognized waltz composer Rodolfo Campodónico, born in Hermosillo in 1866. He garnered a lot of recognition for his work during the early 20th century and his nickname was “Champ,” and that is from where the hotel took its name.

According to recent reports, champ celebrates the desert, the city, the local spirit and Sonoran traditions. Using imagery from old postcards and photos found in basements and thrift shops, its aim is to be as cozy and comfortable as possible for its guests.

Sources indicate that the muted color palette was inspired by the arid northern Mexican region, where the vastness of the land and the sky reign supreme. A retro typography was chosen, since the old house where Champ is located was built in the 1970s.

Auto racing’s seen an explosion of flimsy “fashion wheel” brands that pretend to be high-performance. Apex is different — engineering elite racing wheels at an unmatched price point. But when we met them, customers were completely unaware of the difference. Working closely with their CEO, Eddy Pintacsi, we developed a latest category vision and brand, positioning them as the category leader they are, and injecting some much-needed truth into the wheel industry.

We started by naming the problem that Apex solves, calling it The Great Knowledge Void. A state of play where any wheel brand can make performance claims — true or not — just to make a buck. And the worst part? Customers have no way to know the difference. We went on to tell a story of how Apex is fixing this problem with their core ethos: “Real performance.” A pledge to show customers the truth — or die trying. End of story.

According to recent reports, the identity is loud and urgent. To stop people from buying bogus wheels. The arching curves and high-contrast colors catch the eyes on the track — where it matters. And we worked with Apex to weave the same sense of urgency into how they talk about their testing standards. So that the entire industry would get with the program.

Altogether, the rebrand, POV, and messaging proves that Apex stands alone in its category. We call this a “Category of One” brand. Because when you risk everything on the track, there’s only one thing you can trust — Real Performance.

It’s Selfish, It’s Hokey, and I’ll Lose My Edge: 3 Half-Truths About Self-Compassion

💡 Key Takeaways
  • I’m a late adopter of a lot of things.
  • It has been revealed that why such reluctance to embrace the research-backed practice of self-compassion?
  • We think that being kind to ourselves is self-indulgent and self-focused.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I’m a late adopter of a lot of things. It took me two years to get an iPhone, a lot of convincing to wear AirPods (which I still call ear pods despite my son’s cringe), and it took me even longer to drink the “self-compassion” Kool-Aid. (Which I guess I drank because I wrote a book on how to practice self-compassion daily!).

It has been revealed that why such reluctance to embrace the research-backed practice of self-compassion? I believed three things about self-compassion that turned me off. But I’ve since learned, they are really only half-truths.

We think that being kind to ourselves is self-indulgent and self-focused. Yet the research reveals that when you practice self-compassion, you are more likely to:.

If you are a parent, you probably know this firsthand. When you practice caring for yourself, you are less likely to have your stress spill over onto your kids. But there is a half-truth to self-compassion making you selfish.

According to recent reports, in other words, if you are worried that self-compassion will make you selfish, focus more on how giving yourself compassion will help you be of service to others. One body-based practice I like to do with this concept is a simple breathing exercise:.

Breathing in, I take in care and understanding.Breathing out, I send out care and understanding.

There is a large body of research showing that self-compassion actually helps you perform better, not worse.

Self-compassion helps you stay on track with your wisest values and goals. The half-truth? When you practice self-compassion you may choose to lose your edge a little…in good ways.

As you learn to listen more to your body and stop berating yourself for mistakes, you naturally may want to give up on pushing yourself in ways that are harmful. I’ve lost my edge when it comes to having to run every day, getting every email returned in a timely manner, and making the perfect dinner for my family (hello Trader Joe’s frozen aisle!) … and that’s a good thing.

It has been revealed that when my clients are struggling with whether or not they should push themselves at something, I ask them to do what contemplative leader Stephen Batchelor suggested to me: Drop the question into your belly. If you struggle with self-criticism or rigid rules, your belly is likely to have a more compassionate answer than your head!

It can feel uncomfortable to say nice things to yourself, and sometimes downright cheesy. I rarely recommend clients cheer themselves on with the “Good job” or “Way to go!” statements that some motivational coaches suggest.

Industry observers note that self-compassion is relating to yourself in a way that is encouraging, warm, realistic, and just right for you. You don’t need to recite a list of loving-kindness mantras or put your hand on your heart if you find those practices hokey. Sometimes self-compassion is as simple as noticing the part of you that is scared and being with it a little longer.

In a recent development, the half-truth? When you practice self-compassion, you just might start to adopt some hokey platitudes toward yourself. But hey, they are platitudes for a good reason, right?

It has been revealed that to learn more about how to bring self-compassion into your daily life, read The Self-Compassion Daily Journal by Dr. Diana Hill or listen to the Wise Effort Podcast.

  • Many of the Wallis paintings—of tilted houses and harbours, ships and stormy seas, under lowering grey skies—originally acquired as gifts or bought for a few shillings, are now being borrowed from private collections and museums including the Tate, Kettle’s Yard in Cambridge and Aberdeen Art Gallery.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, pallant House Gallery in Chichester, southern England, does not own any paintings by the self-taught Cornish artist Alfred Wallis (1855-1942). But it does own many works by the early 20th-century artists who were heavily influenced by the former fisherman and rag-and-bone merchant, who first took up painting with pots of house paint and sheets of cardboard as a lonely widower aged 70.

Industry observers note that alfred Wallis: an Artists’ Artist gathers together works by Wallis and by artists who visited, lived in or worked in St Ives, including Barbara Hepworth, Peter Lanyon, Margaret Mellis, Adrian Stokes, John Wells, Wilhelmina Barns-Graham, Ben and Winifred Nicholson and Christopher Wood. It was Ben Nicholson and Wood who first befriended Wallis in 1928 when they peered in astonishment into his tiny dark cottage stuffed with paintings.

Many of the Wallis paintings—of tilted houses and harbours, ships and stormy seas, under lowering grey skies—originally acquired as gifts or bought for a few shillings, are now being borrowed from private collections and museums including the Tate, Kettle’s Yard in Cambridge and Aberdeen Art Gallery. A private collector is loaning a unique collaborative work: a half-finished view of a Brittany quayside by Christopher Wood, which Wood gave to Wallis who then completed it.

A record price of £184,000 was set at a Christie’s auction last year for a work by Wallis, who once said to a buyer: “gimme what you like for ’em”. Ben Nicholson, barely earning himself and with a young family, bought his first Wallis painting for half a crown; Wallis once sent a bundle of paintings to the collector and curator Jim Ede for ten shillings. When the artist died in 1942, a roll of uncashed postal orders was found on his mantelpiece. He was only saved from a pauper’s grave by the St Ives artists.

Winifred Nicholson’s Seascape with Two Boats (1932) Photo: © Kettle’s Yard, University of Cambridge; © Trustees of Winifred Nicholson.

The exhibition is curated by James Scott, an orthopaedic surgeon, who first discovered Wallis when, as a bored medical student, he spent days in Sotheby’s auction rooms, watching sales and afterwards tracing the buyers out of curiosity.

Scott insists there was neither condescension nor exploitation in the relationship between Wallis and Nicholson and the other art school educated artists. Hepworth wrote that Wallis never knew “how much we all learnt from him”.

The St Ives artists “discovered him when they were looking for a newly introduced direction, experimenting with a restricted palette and flattened picture plane,” Scott indicates, “and they found he was already doing it and doing it better.” Wallis learned nothing from them, continuing his own unmistakable style until weeks before his death.

Scott treasures two works by Wallis. “I’ve often thought maybe the time has come to sell them, and then I come downstairs and see them on the wall and think no, I can’t, I love them more and more.”.

• Alfred Wallis: an Artists’ Artist, Pallant House Gallery, Chichester, 21 November-2 May 2027; Penlee House, Penzance, 15 May 2027-9 October 2027.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Dinner Ladies needed a recipe for a rebrand that would not only pay respect to their unique origin story but bring their visual and verbal identity up to speed with their growth as Australia’s tastiest frozen meal service. We joined forces to cook them up a fresh look and feel that reflects their homely meals and anti-“mumsy” attitude, extending all the way from their website through to their packaging. Now whack the oven on, because Australia’s hottest frozen meal service has arrived.

Industry observers note that since it all began with two determined women in a Sydney-side backyard shed in 2007, The Dinner Ladies have been filling the freezers, bellies and hearts of thousands of busy Australian families with their ready-to-heat comfort meals. Born from a deep understanding of dinner time chaos, and the desire to bring some ease back into this routine, The Dinner Ladies’ commitment to delivering meals worthy of mum’s tick of approval remains unwavering.

In a recent development, the market for pre-prepared meal delivery is an oversaturated landscape steeped in clichés and same-same messaging that claims to be the most healthy, convenient or delicious dinnertime solution. They not only lack a distinct personality but also relatability to their customer — time-poor people who just want simple, genuinely good, homemade meals that help take the pressure off when it’s needed most. This is where The Dinner Ladies shine. A flavour-stacked service that takes care of dinner, so you can focus on doing life.

The brand had become known and loved for their unexpected, no nonsense and slightly audacious approach. This was not only refreshingly real but a reflection of both their wholesome offering and the founding ladies. However, over seventeen years of brand iterations their look had become diluted, lost its attitudinal punch, and needed a big serve of reinvigoration. Our vision was to bring back the best from their history and turn up the heat across the board to let the nation know they mean (meal delivery) business.

According to recent reports, we fully immersed ourselves in The Dinner Ladies story, from taking a deep dive through past website designs and hand drawn logos on a napkin, to visiting the shed where it all began and the factory where it now thrives. This helped us draw out the strongest existing brand elements, like their early trad-tattoo-esque illustrations and counter-“mumsy” stereotype, and turn them into a modern evolution. Driven by “Food from the Heart,” each component of the visual identity communicates the brand essence and no-BS confidence of a service that truly helps take the stress out of dinnertime.

Sources indicate that the first step was the refinement of the logo. By decoupling the heart and the script, we gave it flexibility, made it easier to read at every touchpoint and allowed it to scale as needed. The custom heart logo was designed by us and then, alongside the wordmark, handed to illustrator Jake Foreman to redraw and personalise with his iconic texture and gritty stipple.

The Dinner Ladies’ existing red already had distinct brand attribution in the category so we just refined it with a bright and modern twist. The secondary palette supports our hero red with a balance of warm, approachable and slightly retro hues. When united, the system unlocks a number of interesting and vibrant combinations that are particularly useful across hard-working digital applications.

We used the typeface Denim by Displaay Type Foundry to show off the brand’s confident personality yet retain practicality. Denim Wide’s used in headings and call-to-action applications to command attention, while its regular cut counterpart rounds out the system with a friendly, clean and legible option for subheadings and body copy. With its subtle details, the typeface can be an attention-grabbing hero element that showcases the bold tone of voice but also work alongside more expressive moments.

Industry observers note that the tone of voice needed to capture the brand’s joyful, cheeky yet comforting personality, while steering clear of any patronising “mumsy” tropes and stereotypes. We worked with copywriter Cat Wall to develop a verbal identity that balanced the empathetic caregiver with the charmingly rebellious tone of the ladies themselves. In a category saturated with over-sincerity and fake friendliness, the tone offers a refreshing sprinkle of irreverence with a straight-forward, bull-free reflection of the audience and their needs.

The photography celebrates the authentic messiness of real life dinnertime. A reflection of the brand’s tell-it-like-it-is attitude, the shoot didn’t shy away from capturing raw moments — the remnants of a great dish alongside a upcoming one being served or a bolognese-faced baby — mixed with the joy of sharing generous, mouth-watering food.

With Alana Dimou behind the lens, Jerrie-Joy Redman-Lloyd on styling, Oriana De Luca on wardrobe, Gavin Anesbury with a hair and makeup brush in hand, and Michaela Le on production, the brand came to life. Warm, natural lighting, combined with quirky styling choices, pops of colour or pattern and intentional (and encouraged) chaos set a homely and inviting scene with a pinch of rebellion.

Recent findings suggest that illustration has always been a major piece of The Dinner Ladies’ brand so we wanted to bring it across to the rebrand. The original illustrations’ punk and rough-around-the-edges flair drew us to references of traditional trad tattoos.

Sources indicate that collaborating further with illustrator Jake Foreman, we crafted a suite of illustrations that served as both personality-rich storytelling pieces and functional devices. While the small scenes and spots speak to specific offerings of the brand, the hero illustration speaks to the love behind every Dinner Ladies dish and the comforting shared experiences created around the table.

These illustrations are supported by our suite of type-furniture elements that not only support the main design elements but add character to any layout.

Recent findings suggest that as a product that’s often shoved into the freezer and then reached for in a rush, legibility and easy differentiation were priorities for designing the packaging. A simple colour-coded system helps to distinguish between protein groups at a glance, making it quick and effortless to find the crowd-pleasing meal that’s ready to save the day.

In a recent development, the Dinner Ladies now have a brand that not only celebrates their seventeen year legacy but gives them the tools for future decades of success. The flexible design system and punchy tone of voice pays tribute to their tenacious past, the founding ladies behind the service and their wholesome mission put joy back into dinner time. Now The Dinner Ladies can stand loud and proud with a brand that reflects their readiness to dish up delicious dinners to an entire nation.

The only points path to nonstop business class service to French Polynesia.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ashton was the first restaurant chain in Canada to specialize in poutine – it’s been serving the iconic dish since 1969. However, as the decades passed, both Ashton’s image and its restaurants remained frozen in time. In 2022, Émily Adam and Jean-Christophe Lirette took over the reins from Ashton Leblond, with a vision of expanding the 23 locations of this beloved Quebec brand.

In a recent development, the latest owners faced some major challenges: stagnant sales figures, outdated restaurants, an aging clientele and the need to recruit younger workers. It promptly became clear that Ashton’s brand image and experience needed to be revitalized.

LG2 reimagined Ashton’s entire brand experience at one of its flagship restaurants. Numerous elements were redesigned to simplify the brand as a whole and turn it into an exportable entity.

The experience was updated with a perfect blend of modernity and traditions rooted in Ashton’s history. In tribute to snack bar culture, all the classic codes of diners were integrated with a modern twist. A customized typographic signature emphasizing the generous, indulgent nature of Ashton dishes was created, and the chain’s signature red colour was updated. A touch of nostalgia can be felt in the new brand merchandise, which features illustrations reminiscent of one of Ashton’s earliest logos.

The colours are rich, curved edges are prominent and the triple red line – inspired by the chain’s iconic neon lighting – runs through every touchpoint in the graphic system, from the fresh packaging to the stripes on socks.

To create an atmosphere as comforting as its food, the design concept was completely overhauled. This transformation can be seen from the outer shell to the interior details: the pervasive curves, neon lighting and red tin roof are all reminiscent of Ashton’s original 1969 food truck.

A monochrome red border runs through the dining room where the famous banquettes are still featured prominently in the centre. This easily reproducible layout will be extended to the chain’s other restaurants over the next few years.

Recent findings suggest that the numbers speak for themselves. Within 30 days of launch:.

35% increase in traffic at the first renovated location 34% increase in sales at the first renovated location 40% increase in visits to the Ashton website.

Ashton found the perfect recipe for securing the loyalty of diehard fans while attracting fresh foodies on the hunt for a retro yet contemporary experience.
